facts.statement: Goniopholis resembled living crocodilians and likely functioned as a semi-aquatic ambush predator.
facts.quote: Like other goniopholidids, it resembled living crocodilians, and probably had a similar ecology as semi-aquatic ambush predators.

facts.statement: Unlike modern crocodilians, Goniopholis possessed dermal armor on its back made of two rows of large rectangular scutes with a "peg and groove" articulation mechanism.
facts.quote: However, unlike modern crocodilians and like other goniopholidids, the dermal armour covering the back was composed of two rows of large rectangular scutes running parallel down each side of the midline, with a "peg and groove" mechanism articulating the sets of plates together, with the outer edge of the plates deflected downwards.

facts.statement: The species G. kiplingi was named to honor the author Rudyard Kipling for his enthusiasm for natural sciences.
facts.quote: G. kiplingi honors the author Rudyard Kipling, "in recognition for his enthusiasm for natural sciences".

facts.statement: G. kiplingi had a skull reaching 475.6 mm, making it one of the largest goniopholidids.
facts.quote: G. kiplingi had skull reaching 475.6 mm, it is one of the largest goniopholidid along with Amphicotylus milesi which had skull reaching 43 cm.

facts.statement: Eggs attributed to Goniopholis have been found in the Late Jurassic of Portugal.
facts.quote: Eggs attributed to Goniopholis were found in the Late Jurassic of Portugal.

facts.statement: The type species G. crassidens is known from the Berriasian of England, while the referable species G. simus from the Berriasian of NW Germany might be conspecific.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus is G. crassidens which is known from the Berriasian of England, and the referable species G. simus from the Berriasian of NW Germany, might be conspecific.

facts.statement: G. baryglyphaeus from the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian) of Portugal is the oldest known Goniopholis species.
facts.quote: Other species that are referable to Goniopholis include G. kiplingi from the Berriasian of England, and G. baryglyphaeus from the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian) of Portugal making it the oldest known Goniopholis species.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton of an indeterminate Goniopholis species was recovered from the Berriasian-aged Angeac-Charente bonebed in France.
facts.quote: A partial skeleton of an indeterminate species of Goniopholis has been recovered from the Berriasian aged Angeac-Charente bonebed of France.

facts.statement: Goniopholis has been inferred to be ectothermic based on bone histology and stable isotope analysis.
facts.quote: Goniopholis have been inferred to have been ectothermic on the basis of bone histology and stable isotope analysis.

facts.statement: The genus Goniopholis was named by Richard Owen in 1841.
facts.quote: Category:Taxa named by Richard Owen Category:Fossil taxa described in 1841

facts.statement: Goniopholis belongs to the order Mesoeucrocodylia and the family Goniopholididae.
The species G. phuwiangensis from NE Thailand was reassigned to the genus Sunosuchus.
facts.quote: G. phuwiangensis (Buffetaut & Ingavat, 1983) procedente del noreste de Tailandia, corresponde a una especie conocida por restos fragmentarios y fue reasignada al género Sunosuchus.

facts.statement: The North American species G. lucasii and G. kirtlandicus were reclassified into their own genera, Amphicotylus and Denazinosuchus, respectively.
facts.quote: G. lucasii y G. kirtlandicus fueron reclasificadas en sus propios géneros, Amphicotylus y Denazinosuchus, respectivamente

facts.statement: A complete specimen previously classified as Goniopholis was recently re-described as the new species G. willetti.
facts.quote: Los goniofolídidos de Willett/Hulke, de Hooley y de Dollo representan varios especímenes completos anteriormente clasificados en las especies G. simus o G. crassidens, y una de estas fue redescrita como una nueva especie, G. willetti (Salisbury y Naish, 2011).

facts.statement: Goniopholis lived from the Bathonian to the Santonian, approximately 168.2 to 83.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Santonian (168.2 to 83.6 million years ago)
